content: The Orthodontic Technicians Association (OTA) is the primary professional organization for orthodontic technicians in the United Kingdom. While it is based in the UK, its membership extends internationally, with many of its 312 Fellows, Licentiates, Members, Associate Members, and Honorary Members practicing abroad. In 1971, orthodontic technicians in London began meeting to discuss the regulation and improvement of orthodontic technology standards. Bert Aldridge, the chief orthodontic technician at the Hospital for Sick Children (now Great Ormond Street Hospital), and Len Bradshaw, from King’s College Dental School, initiated discussions about forming an association. Aldridge wrote to orthodontic technicians in London teaching hospitals, and a meeting was held at Great Ormond Street Hospital. Thirteen technicians attended, and it was agreed to form an association. A steering committee was established, with Len Bradshaw as the first chairman and Bert Aldridge as secretary. Other committee members included P. Chittenden, H. Close, J. Ford, J. Griffin, and H. Haringman. By March 1972, aims and objectives were formalized, and a letter and questionnaire were sent to dental schools, hospital orthodontic departments, and county council dental laboratories. The committee members, along with others, contributed to a launching fund to cover initial costs. By July 1972, membership applications were invited, and the first conference was planned for April 1973. The OTA council meets at the headquarters of the British Orthodontic Society at 12 Bridewell Place, London, which opened in 2006. The OTA logo is circular and features the letters OTA alongside an otter, the association’s mascot, due to the phonetic similarity of OTA to otter. The logo is encircled by the words Orthodontic Technicians Association. The association’s goals remain aligned with those of its founders: to promote the study and advancement of orthodontic laboratory and clinical techniques, encourage high standards of practice, and benefit both the orthodontic team and patients. The OTA advises institutions and individuals on orthodontic laboratory techniques and services provided by orthodontic technicians. Membership is divided into several categories: 1. Student Members: Dental technicians in training to specialize in orthodontics or students with an interest in orthodontics. They pay reduced subscription rates, receive the journal, and can attend conferences and meetings but do not have voting rights at the Annual General Meeting (AGM). 2. Associate Members: Individuals with a special interest in orthodontics or those connected to the field. They receive the newsletter and can attend conferences but cannot vote at the AGM. 3. Members: Qualified dental technicians working in orthodontics without a specialist qualification. Members receive the newsletter, can attend conferences, and have voting rights at the AGM. They may also stand for election to the council and use the post-nominal letters MOTA. 4. Licentiates: Those holding advanced qualifications in orthodontics, such as a City & Guilds Advanced Certificate or equivalent. Licentiates have the same rights as Members but can also stand for council election and use the post-nominal letters LOTA. 5. Honorary Members and Fellows: These titles are awarded at the discretion of the council to any grade of member. 6. Retired Members: Members who reach retirement age can pay a reduced subscription rate while retaining the right to attend meetings and conferences and receive all literature. The OTA organizes several events, including its annual conference, which is considered an essential opportunity for dental technicians to stay updated on the latest developments in orthodontic technology. The 2008 conference was scheduled to be held in Edinburgh. The OTA also participates in the British Orthodontic Conference (BOC) and the Dental Technology Show (DTS). The association has established awards to encourage excellence in orthodontics. The British Orthodontic Society Technicians Award, created in 1999, includes a technical workpiece, a free-choice appliance, and a written essay. It is open to students and recently qualified technicians. The Aldridge Medal, launched in 2007 following a donation by Bert Aldridge, recognizes the best lecture presented at the annual conference, as judged by members. The first recipient of the Aldridge Medal was Susan Owen, who was awarded at the 2008 conference. The OTA Council, elected by members, governs the association. It traditionally includes a President (an orthodontist maintaining links with the British Orthodontic Society), four executive council members (Chairman, Secretary, Treasurer, and Membership Secretary), and five non-executive council members. In 2005, two additional non-executive positions were created, bringing the total to 12 council members. Council members serve voluntarily and are responsible for the governance, sustainability, and finances of the OTA. They represent the interests of orthodontic technicians on various boards and committees, including the British Orthodontic Society, British Standards Institution, General Dental Council, and others. In 2002, the OTA council was featured on the BBC News website in an article about kilts following a conference in Stirling. Members featured included Bob Woods, John Windibank, Ed Payne, John Brown, Gavin Carmichael, Paul Mallett, and Chris Bridle.
